n: Luke opens his second volume by addressing Theophilus again. His “former treatise” — the Gospel of Luke — told what Jesus began to do and teach; Acts tells what the risen Lord continued doing through his apostles and the Holy Ghost.

f.g: Greek for “friend of God” or “loved by God”; probably a real patron, perhaps a Roman official.

n: The Gospel ran until Jesus was taken up to heaven, after he had instructed his chosen apostles through the Holy Ghost.

f.w: the apostles whom he had chosen

n: After his suffering, Jesus proved he was alive with many convincing evidences, appearing to them over forty days and teaching about God’s kingdom.

f.g: passion = suffering, especially Christ’s suffering and death.
Forty is a biblical number of preparation.

n: While eating with them, he commanded them to stay in Jerusalem and wait for what the Father had promised — the gift of the Holy Ghost.
John baptized with water, but in a few days they would be baptized with the Holy Ghost. Latter-day Saints see these as two parts of one baptism — of water and of the Spirit.
The apostles ask whether he will now restore the kingdom to Israel — still hoping for national, political deliverance.

f.w: restore again the kingdom to Israel

n: Jesus replies that the timing of such events is the Father’s business, not theirs to know.

Instead they will receive power when the Holy Ghost comes, and be his witnesses in widening circles — Jerusalem, Judea, Samaria, and to the ends of the earth. This verse outlines the whole book of Acts.

f.w: ye shall be witnesses unto me
unto the uttermost part of the earth

n: As they watch, he is lifted up and a cloud hides him from view. Clouds often signal God’s presence in scripture.

f.w: a cloud received him out of their sight

n: While they stare into the sky, two men in white — angels — appear beside them.

f.w: two men stood by them in white apparel

n: The angels ask why the Galileans stand gazing upward: this same Jesus will return in the same way they saw him go. His Second Coming will be personal, visible, and glorious.

f.w: shall so come in like manner

n: They return to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, a short walk — about two-thirds of a mile.

f.g: The distance the rabbis allowed one to walk on the Sabbath: about 2,000 cubits, roughly 0.6 miles (1 km).

n: They go to the upper room where they are staying. Luke lists the eleven remaining apostles — the Twelve minus Judas Iscariot.

f.g: “The Zealot,” possibly once part of a movement zealous for Jewish independence.

n: They all pray together with one heart — along with faithful women, Mary the mother of Jesus (her last mention in the Bible), and Jesus’s brothers, who now believe.

f.g: with one accord = united in mind and purpose.

n: During those days Peter, now leading, stands up among about 120 believers.
Peter says scripture spoken by the Holy Ghost through David had to be fulfilled concerning Judas, who guided those who arrested Jesus.
Judas had been one of them, sharing in their ministry — which makes his fall all the more tragic.

Luke adds a parenthetical note on Judas’s grim end: the field bought with his betrayal money became the place where he fell and his body burst open. Matthew says Judas hanged himself; many readers harmonize the two accounts by supposing his body later fell.
Everyone in Jerusalem knew of it, and the field was called Akeldama, “Field of Blood,” in their local Aramaic.
Peter quotes two Psalms: one about the betrayer’s home becoming deserted, and one about another taking his office.

f.g: bishoprick = office or position of oversight.

n: So a replacement must come from those who had been with them throughout the Lord’s ministry.
The replacement must have been with them from John’s baptism to the Ascension, to be ordained as a witness of the Resurrection — the core of an apostle’s calling.

f.w: a witness with us of his resurrection

n: They put forward two candidates: Joseph called Barsabbas (also known as Justus) and Matthias.

f.g: A Latin name meaning “just, righteous.” Using multiple names was common.

n: They pray to the Lord, who knows every heart, asking him to show which one he has chosen. The choice is the Lord’s, not theirs.

f.w: which knowest the hearts of all men
shew whether of these two thou hast chosen

n: The chosen one will take the place in the apostolic ministry that Judas abandoned through transgression to go “to his own place.”

f.g: A sober phrase for the destiny Judas chose for himself.

n: They cast lots, and the lot falls to Matthias, who is added to the eleven. The Quorum of the Twelve is kept full — a pattern Latter-day Saints see continued in the restored Church.

f.g: Casting lots was a traditional way of seeking God’s decision; it is never used again after the Spirit is poured out.
